blocks.text: Four parts build the case for the strategy in Chapter 3. Section 2.1 draws lessons from comparator destinations; sections 2.2, 2.3 and 2.4 then examine demand, supply and the enabling environment, on which Pillars 1, 2 and 3 rest.

Demand is not what holds the province back. Its shape and the system that serves it do. Five markets and six months carry most overseas visits, and seats into Cape Town run out at the peak. Beyond the Metro, product is hard to reach and book, and in townships and rural settlements the missing piece is a local seller. The institutions that should hold the system together have thinned. Section 2.1 first shows how the fastest growers dealt with their own binding constraint.

Stakeholder evidence runs through sections 2.2 to 2.4. The first of four engagement phases ran from January to March 2026 (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p4, p17; the record of the three later phases is not yet in hand). In it, 16 organisations from Mossel Bay to the CTICC gave 223 rated insights: 115 High, 102 Medium and 6 Low (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p20 to p46, counted). Each stakeholder statement in this chapter is the project team's paraphrase of a point an organisation made, attributed to that organisation and never to a person. [Open item: each organisation named here to approve its paraphrase before publication.] Each part ends with a box, "What this means for the strategy", which sets out what the part's evidence means for the focus areas it touches.
2.1 Global benchmarks and their lessons

The destinations that grew fastest ran institutions, marketing and air access as one system aimed at a single binding constraint. For the Western Cape that constraint is seats into one gateway; in its townships and rural settlements it is the lack of a local seller.
Benchmarks test the strategy against proven growth

The province aims to double international arrivals by 2035 (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p6). Growth above trend is rare across whole regions; where it happens, it is specific to a destination (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p7). Benchmarking asks which deliberate choices let comparable destinations outgrow the world, and which of them the Western Cape can adapt. It looks for how each destination removed what bound its growth, not for isolated good practice (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p6).

The yardstick is the world's own growth. Growth of 3% to 5% a year is the norm under stable conditions; above 5% marks structural acceleration and 10% or more a structural shift (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p7). UN Tourism puts global growth at 11% in 2024, while recovery was still running, and about 4% in 2025 (World Tourism Barometer, Jan 2025 and Jan 2026). Growth counts as structural only when it is "driven by deliberate changes to demand drivers, access conditions or product systems, rather than cyclical recovery or short-term promotion" (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p8). Each case was read for its demand profile, two proven growth levers and how far they transfer to the Western Cape (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p13).
Six comparators from a screen of 30

The search began with more than 25 destinations across Africa, Europe, the Americas and Oceania, and 30 were scored against 12 criteria in four groups (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p29 to p31; Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p11, p12). Market and access asks whether visitors arrive as the Western Cape's do, by long-haul air through hubs from the same markets. Destination and product structure asks whether a gateway city leads into several regions with a similar mix and price. Growth and inclusion compares growth stage, seasonality, community participation and climate pressure; performance compares volume, yield and infrastructure (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p30; Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p11). Appendix A3 lists all twelve.

Each destination received one average score across the twelve criteria, and the 30 were ranked on it (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p29, p31). Four of the final six were among the six the screen judged most closely aligned: Chile, Melbourne and Victoria, Valencia and Singapore (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p32; Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p12). Below them, partial likeness ruled destinations out. Namibia lacks city, wine and cultural depth. Reykjavik and Iceland sell one nature product with extreme seasonality, and the Eastern Cape and Garden Route have no long-haul hub or global brand role (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p31).

Score alone did not settle the set. The other two places went to New Zealand, ranked seventh at 3.67, and Kenya, ranked eleventh at 3.50 (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p31; Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p12). Porto and Vancouver, which the screen had placed in its top six, did not make the set, and no reason is recorded (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p32; Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p12). The screen had judged New Zealand less aligned on source markets and cruise, and Kenya weaker on wine and agri-tourism, with different pricing and governance (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p31). Kenya's inclusion was meant to make the set more balanced and regionally grounded (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p62). New Zealand's comparability rests on access: like the Western Cape it is remote, long-haul and entered through one gateway (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p51). Wesgro and the project team were to settle the list together (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p66).

The six cover the constraints the province faces. Chile and New Zealand show how a gateway wins long-haul seats and fills them; Singapore and Kenya show how hub traffic becomes visits. Melbourne shows how events spread demand across the year, and Valencia how quality is governed.

blocks.text: Community cases and peer airports answer narrower questions

Five community cases ask what keeps tourism income in townships and rural settlements. Each matches one of four types among the province's 107 long-listed communities (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p4, p14, p15). The types turn on two facts: whether a community lies within 45 minutes of a tourism node, and whether it holds an attraction. Vilakazi Street, Santa Marta in Rio de Janeiro and Kliptown speak to communities near a node. Costa Rica's rural network and Comuna 13 in Medellín, remote by access rather than distance, speak to remote ones (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p15).

Cape Town's route record was set against eight peer airports: Calgary, Christchurch, Edinburgh, Keflavik, Larnaca, Marrakech, Santiago and Valencia. Five are not their country's main airport, and most serve seasonal or fast-growing inbound leisure markets (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "International Comparisons", counted). Santiago and Christchurch share Cape Town's remote geography, and Santiago targets tripling its passenger volumes in twenty years (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "International Comparisons").
Cape Town wins more mainline routes than its peers

Between 2015 and 2025 Cape Town added 17 mainline international services, more than any of the eight peer airports (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "International Comparisons"). Santiago added 14 services, Valencia 12 and Calgary 8 (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "Executive Summary", "International Comparisons"; other study documents count new routes from 2014 on a different basis). Yet winning routes is not the same as holding seats through the winter, and the routes won now run full (section 2.3). Low-cost carriers tell a different story: Edinburgh added 121 routes from 2015 to 2025, and low-cost carriers fly 81% of its routes (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "Executive Summary", "International Comparisons"). At Cape Town, low-cost entry "would be a longer term opportunity" (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "International Comparisons"). The Western Cape does not need to learn how to win mainline routes. It needs what the leaders added: access funded as infrastructure and marketing tied to each route.
Fast growth in 2024 was partly recovery

Only Chile and Singapore grew far faster than the world in 2024: Chile by 40.4% and Singapore by 21%, against the world's 11% (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p9; Sernatur, Dec 2025; Singapore Tourism Board, Feb 2025). Neither rate proves structural growth. Singapore was still at 86% of its 2019 arrivals, and most of Chile's arrivals came overland, 40% of them from Argentina (Sernatur, Dec 2025; Singapore Tourism Board, Feb 2025). Kenya, Valencia and New Zealand grew only slightly faster than the world, and Melbourne's 4.3% is an Australia-wide forecast rather than an actual (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p9, p17, p53; the 12% shown for New Zealand matches its 2025 holiday-arrivals growth, with total arrivals up 5.9%). The lessons that follow come from what the leaders built over a decade, not from one year's rate.
The Western Cape should apply the same test to its own record: growth counts when deliberate change drives it, not when recovery returns lost visitors (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p8).
What each comparator faced and what it did
Chile built access first

Chile was chosen as a long-haul city gateway to coast, wine and wilderness, with Mediterranean seasons like the Western Cape's (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p12, p22). South America supplies 55% to 60% of its arrivals (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p24). Yet long-haul access was its binding constraint, and Chile treated it as infrastructure (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p59). Santiago's airport traffic rose from about 16 million passengers in 2010 to more than 26 million in 2019 (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p24, p25; the source prints about 90% to 95% of 5.2 million international arrivals through Santiago, which can hold only for air arrivals, since land borders carried 55.6% in 2024). A private concession won in 2015 funded about US$900 million of expansion, under one of the world's most liberal aviation systems built on open-skies agreements (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p23, p26). Direct routes now link Santiago with Europe and Australia, and a domestic network carries visitors on to Patagonia and the wine valleys (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p25, p26). The lesson is blunt: "Tourism demand follows air access" (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p25).
New Zealand tied marketing to routes

New Zealand holds coast, wine, nature and culture within short travel distances, as the Western Cape does (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p51). Air access economics bind its growth (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p51). It "shifted from awareness-driven marketing to route accountable demand generation", tying budgets to specific long-haul corridors and designing campaigns around airline breakeven and shoulder-season loads (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p54). The programme reports more than 16,000 incremental bookings and a return of about NZ$55 million in 2023/24. Government-backed early-stage route incentives and data shared between tourism bodies and airlines support it (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p54). In the regions it curates premium multi-day circuits and limits capacity to protect price (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p55).
Singapore turned a hub into a destination

Singapore was chosen for joining air access, service quality, food culture and visitor segmentation in one approach (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p12). Its question was how to turn transit through Changi into stays. Its answer is a stopover programme, with the tourism board, Changi Airport Group and Singapore Airlines working "under a coordinated strategy" (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p40). It received 16.5 million international visitors in 2024 and record tourism receipts of about S$29 billion (Singapore Tourism Board, Feb 2025). A hotel transformation map and fund lifted quality alongside, moving Singapore "from lower-value stopover visits toward longer stays and higher-value tourism spending" (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p41).
Kenya made wildlife a governed system

Kenya is the African case, chosen for its long-haul reliance, regional dispersal and community-based tourism (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p12). African markets supply 41% of its arrivals, while long-haul visitors spend more per head (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p32). Kenya "institutionalised conservation as national economic infrastructure", joining wildlife protection, tourism and community participation in one governed system (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p33). It positioned Nairobi as East Africa's aviation, diplomatic and business hub, and its main airport now carries 68% of arrivals (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p32, p34). Despite meaningful reforms, fragmented investment and regulatory hurdles remain ongoing challenges (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p31). Kenya earned about US$1,460 per international arrival in 2024, against about US$890 for the Western Cape (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p15).
Melbourne and Victoria fill the year with events

Melbourne plays the part for Victoria that Cape Town plays for the province: main point of entry, brand anchor and engine of demand (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p15). Summer still brings the largest spike in international demand, so Victoria curates a portfolio of events that "generate repeat, predictable demand spikes across the year" (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p17, p18). Behind the calendar, hotel stock grew 21%, about 5,000 rooms (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p18). Melbourne "uses its event calendar to de-risk and stimulate aviation demand" (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p59). Its monthly share of arrivals ranges only from 7% in June and July to 12% in December (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p17). Its case rests on stability and yield rather than speed.
Valencia governed quality across the destination

Valencia, a coastal city of culture and food, matches the province on climate, product mix and price (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p12). It faced a familiar problem: fragmented governance and uneven quality across regions, operators and seasons (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p46). It adopted a destination-wide quality system across its tourism businesses (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p47). Coordination sits in "a permanent public-private structure led by Visit València", which joins municipal, provincial and regional authorities in one decision-making system (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p47). It received 3.5 million international visitors in 2024, 13.9% more than in 2023 and 24.4% above 2019. Spend rose faster still, by 21% (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p46).
The leaders treat air access as infrastructure

The Western Cape faces both halves of the access problem Chile and New Zealand attacked: too few seats at the peak and thin demand off it. On the growth model, the base case passes a line of 1.8 million inbound seats by 2030 (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p20). That line is the model's assumption; in practice the runway binds at peak hours (section 2.3). Off-peak, June carries only 6.4% of the year's international capacity (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "Seasonality").

The two cases point to three changes. Air access should be treated as "core economic infrastructure, not a tourism add-on", with "a permanent, well-funded Public-Private Air Access Fund" (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p28). The province should "actively lobby for air service liberalisation and simplified visa regimes" (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p28). Marketing budgets should be ring-fenced around priority long-haul corridors, with an aviation partnership framework and early-stage route support (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p56).
Transit and events can be turned into demand

Hubs can be converted into visits, as Singapore and Kenya show. Cape Town's seven largest international markets are all hub airports (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "The Capetown Market"). Government, aviation, events and industry should work to shared KPIs, linking air access, major events and joint marketing (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p42). City, provincial and national actors should align around one gateway strategy, with MICE treated as a system lever (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p35).

Events do the same work across the calendar, and the Western Cape has the green-season gap they address (section 2.2). The province needs one event acquisition and calendar strategy across Wesgro, the Convention Bureau, the City and the Province, with conference bidding aligned to sector strengths (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p20).
Quality and value are governed, not encouraged

The leaders manage quality as a deliberate outcome. Valencia and Singapore set standards through standing bodies rather than leaving them to operators (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p41, p47). The results reported for Singapore include longer stays and higher spend per visitor; those for Valencia include more consistent service, a stronger reputation and more repeat visits (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p41, p47).

The cases ask the Western Cape first for a province-wide quality and standards framework led by Wesgro (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p42). Within it would sit a provincial quality charter phased by district, with certification "visible across booking platforms", alongside standing sector councils for wine, MICE, adventure and culture (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p49). The cases also ask the province to measure its regions by yield rather than arrivals and to build conservation and community inclusion into the offer (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p35, p55, p56).
In communities, lasting sellers matter more than capital

In communities the binding constraint is the seller. The five cases show that local sellers outlast the programmes that launch them (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p7 to p11). In Santa Marta in Rio de Janeiro, about 20 resident guides ran the tours by 2015 and outside jeep firms had left. The guides kept selling after the launch programme ended, while assets and training without a route to market did not last (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p7, p30). Access and safety were preconditions, not product.

Scale brings its own limits. Medellín's Comuna 13 drew 1.98 million visitors in 2025, 52% of them international, with about 300 professional guides. Mobility built for residents became the stage, but carrying-capacity limits came late (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p8). On Vilakazi Street in Soweto, ten restaurants employ more than 800 people. Public space upgrades amplify existing assets, but benefits concentrate on street-front owners (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p9).

Neither capital nor donor money lasts without a seller that can stand alone. Costa Rica's community network turned over more than USD 800,000 in 2013 and dissolved at the end of 2018; it did not survive donor exit, though the record names no single cause (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p10). Kliptown in Soweto received a first allocation of R436 million and was projected to draw almost 200,000 international visitors a year. By 2017 its museum drew about 4,000 visitors a year, because capital built before an operator yields no operating income (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p11).

The cases converge on one order: "a seller with a stake, a safe and workable visit, product that keeps spend in the community, then exposure" (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p12). In the Western Cape's communities, the seller therefore comes before the asset (section 2.4). In Doringbaai and Elands Bay, a local entity comes before more product, with its own selling channel and a succession plan that does not rest on a donor (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p10). Assets follow proven demand (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p31).
The system matters more than any lever

No single lever explains the leaders' growth. Sustained tourism growth "is not created by fragmented interventions, but by a coordinated destination system in which governance, demand generation and access reinforce one another" (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p58). Chile's coordination works best "when anchored around a single strategic constraint" (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p59). The Western Cape's constraint has the same shape as Chile's long-haul access: seats into one gateway airport (section 2.3).

Yet coordination is hard everywhere. Victoria reports tension between national and state bodies over roles and branding (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p16). Valencia struggles to join its data across institutions (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p45). The Western Cape's three tiers of government show the same strain (section 2.4). The strategy should anchor on one constraint, as Chile did: peak seats into Cape Town first, one system built around them and, in the communities, a seller before any asset.
What the comparison cannot show

The cases show what worked elsewhere; they cannot prove it will work here. Singapore's tourism board answers to one ministry, in a system strongly directed by the state yet closely tied to the private sector (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p38). The Western Cape works across three tiers, and air rights and visas sit with national government (section 2.4). New Zealand's governance differs too, and transfer means adapting governance, data and capability to local realities (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p51).

The evidence also has gaps. No score by criterion is printed, and among the six only New Zealand (3.67) and Kenya (3.50) have a printed score (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p31; Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p12). The margins behind the final choice cannot be checked. No case of failure was studied. [Open item: add one comparator that underperformed, as the Inception Report's plan asked (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p16).] Several comparator charts are unlabelled, so only printed figures are quoted here, and Valencia's figures name no primary source (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p24, p39, p46, p53). The recommended air access fund carries no amount (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p28). None of the cases holds Western Cape data, so the province's side of each comparison comes from sections 2.2 to 2.4. The direction of the lessons is robust; the precise rates are indicative.

blocks.title: What this means for the strategy
paras: **Supplies precedent for FA07, Win direct routes and add seats on full routes, and FA15, Crowd in capital with targeted investment strategies.** Chile's airport concession and air access fund; New Zealand's route-tied marketing.

**Supplies precedent for FA04, Convert India and China hub traffic, and FA06, Build a regional foundation (Africa).** Singapore's joint strategy with its airport and airline; Kenya's hub strategy and African base.
**Supplies precedent for FA02, Create green-season demand with MICE and events.** Melbourne's events-led system and unified calendar.
**Supplies precedent for FA10, Support diversified route and product development.** Chile's regional portfolio; New Zealand's premium circuits.

**Supplies precedent for FA11, Align visitor experience in-destination, and FA03, Make the whole province findable and bookable.** Valencia's governed quality and certification visible on booking platforms.

**Supplies precedent for FA05, Increase yield in mature markets, FA12, Balance impact on nature-based attractions, and FA14, Manage climate risk and sustainable tourism.** Yield-based metrics, capacity discipline and conservation-led product.

**Supports FA16, Align institutional stakeholders across all three tiers, FA17, Strengthen industry and government collaboration, and FA18, Expedite tourism-enabling policy and data sharing.** One coordinated system of governance, marketing and access, with shared data between tourism bodies and airlines.
**Supplies precedent for FA19, Lead removal of infrastructure, visa and safety deficits.** Chile's open skies; safety before product in the community cases.
**Supplies precedent for FA20, Develop workforce and service skills.** Singapore's hotel quality drive; the province's own labour analysis is still to be commissioned.

**Supplies precedent for FA13, Embed local destination bodies for community inclusion.** Resident sellers outlasted the programmes that launched them, and capital built before an operator, as in Kliptown, earned no operating income.
